title: Testing Your Own Code - Live Edge-Case Discipline
summary: Interviewers grade how you find your own bugs, not just whether the code has any. Build a standing edge-case checklist, dry-run code by hand, and fix root causes instead of patching symptoms.

slides.markdown:
Interviewers grade **how you find your own bugs**, not just whether the final code happens to have any. A candidate who writes buggy code, then catches and fixes it live through a deliberate test pass, often scores higher than one who writes cleaner code but declares it done without checking anything.

This is because bug-free-on-the-first-try is mostly luck under interview time pressure, while a visible, repeatable process for finding your own mistakes is a skill that transfers to every problem you'll ever debug - including the ones you can't fully solve in forty-five minutes.

This topic covers what to actually test, how to dry-run code by hand without wasting minutes, and the discipline of fixing the real cause instead of patching the symptom you happened to find.

Before declaring any solution done, run it mentally against a short, standing list of edge cases - the same five or six, every time, until checking them is automatic:

- **Empty input** - does the function even handle a length-zero array or string?
- **A single element** - is "the pair," "the window," or "the balanced tree" even well-defined at size one?
- **All duplicates** - does a solution that assumes distinct values quietly break?
- **Already sorted, or reverse-sorted** - does an algorithm that expects disorder degrade or misbehave on already-ordered input?
- **Negative or zero values** - if the problem allows them, does a sum, a product, or an index calculation go wrong?

This list isn't exhaustive for every problem, but running it by default catches a large fraction of interview bugs in under thirty seconds.

slides.sectionTitle: Dry-running your own code out loud
slides.markdown:
Before declaring a solution finished, **trace it by hand on a small, real example**, saying each step out loud rather than silently eyeballing the code and assuming it's right.

Pick an example small enough to trace in your head or on paper in under a minute - three to five elements is usually enough to exercise the interesting logic without burning your remaining time. Walk each variable's value forward one line at a time: "left starts at 0, right at 4... windowSum is 12, that's over target, so I shrink from the left... windowSum drops to 9, still checking."

This catches a specific class of bug that reading the code silently misses: the code *looks* right because you already know what you intended it to do, and your eyes skip past the line where intention and implementation diverge. Saying the actual values out loud forces you to trust the trace, not your memory of the plan.

slides.subTitle: Where an off-by-one hides
slides.markdown:
An off-by-one error is almost always invisible from reading the code and immediately obvious from tracing it, because the bug lives in the gap between what a boundary condition *looks* like it does and what it actually does on a specific small input.

A loop written as `for i in range(len(arr) - 1)` intending to compare every adjacent pair reads as correct at a glance - it *feels* like it should cover the whole array. Tracing it on a 4-element array by hand, index by index, is what actually reveals whether the last pair got included or silently dropped.

slides.markdown:
The most common testing gap: re-running only the **exact example the interviewer originally gave you**, confirming it still works, and declaring the solution done.

The interviewer's example was chosen to explain the problem clearly, not to stress it - it's usually a clean, well-behaved case that every reasonable-looking approach passes, buggy or not. Passing it tells you almost nothing about whether your edge-case handling is correct, because the original example likely never exercised those edges in the first place.

Treat the interviewer's example as your first test, not your last. After it passes, move immediately to the standing edge-case checklist and at least one case you constructed yourself that's different in shape from the given one - a longer input, a different value distribution, an edge the original example didn't touch.

slides.sectionTitle: Reading for your own bug classes
slides.markdown:
A generic bug checklist helps, but the highest-value check is personal: **you already know which mistakes you tend to make**, if you've paid attention across enough practice problems.

Some candidates consistently get loop boundaries wrong (`<` versus `<=`). Others consistently forget to update a variable inside a branch that only sometimes executes. Others mix up which of two similar-looking variables holds the running answer versus the current candidate. These are personal, repeatable patterns, not random chance.

After every practice session, note the specific bug you shipped and its shape, not just that a bug existed. Over time this becomes a short, genuinely personal checklist - three or four items - that you run through specifically, in addition to the generic edge cases, because it's the one list that's calibrated to what you, specifically, are likely to get wrong.

slides.subTitle: When the written trace earns its time cost
slides.markdown:
Two ways to dry-run your code, with a real time trade-off between them:

- **Mentally simulating.** Fast - a few seconds per case - and enough for simple logic you can hold entirely in your head, like a straightforward single-pass loop with one or two variables.
- **Writing the trace out** - a small table of variable values per iteration. Slower to set up, but it catches bugs that mental simulation reliably misses once there are three or more variables changing together, or once the logic branches in a way that's easy to lose track of silently.

The judgment call: reach for a written trace specifically when you notice yourself about to lose track of a variable's value, or when the interviewer looks unconvinced by a mental walk-through. Writing three lines on the whiteboard to settle a doubt is a better use of ninety seconds than confidently mis-stating that the code is correct and having it fail on their hidden test.

slides.sectionTitle: Patching the symptom vs. fixing the cause
slides.markdown:
When a dry run surfaces a bug, the fast, tempting fix is patching it at the exact input where you noticed it - adding a special-case check for the specific value that broke, rather than asking why the general logic produced a wrong answer there.

"It failed when the array had one element, so I'll add `if len(arr) == 1: return arr[0]`" might make that one test pass while leaving the same root cause ready to break on the next input that happens to trigger it a different way - a two-element array with both elements equal, say.

Before patching, ask **why** the bug happened, not just where: was it an off-by-one in a loop bound, an uninitialized variable, a comparison operator facing the wrong direction? Fixing that root cause usually fixes the one-element case too, without adding a special-case branch that only defers the same bug to the next input shape.

slides.subTitle: What a thirty-second dry run looks like
slides.markdown:
```
def max_subarray_sum(nums, k):
    window_sum = sum(nums[:k])
    best = window_sum
    for i in range(k, len(nums)):
        window_sum += nums[i] - nums[i - k]
        best = max(best, window_sum)
    return best

# Trace on nums = [2, 1, 5, 1, 3, 2], k = 3:
# window_sum starts at 2+1+5 = 8, best = 8
# i=3: window_sum += nums[3] - nums[0] = 1 - 2 -> 7,  best stays 8
# i=4: window_sum += nums[4] - nums[1] = 3 - 1 -> 9,  best -> 9
# i=5: window_sum += nums[5] - nums[2] = 2 - 5 -> 6,  best stays 9
# returns 9 - matches the window [5, 1, 3]
```

The trace took four lines and confirmed both the sliding update and the max-tracking are correct - cheaper than debugging a wrong answer after the interviewer runs their own test.

slides.subTitle: Budgeting the last few minutes
slides.markdown:
There's a real trade-off between testing thoroughly and running out of interview time entirely - the goal isn't to test forever, it's to spend the last two or three minutes catching the bugs most likely to be there.

A workable budget: the interviewer's original example first, confirming the happy path still works after any late edits. Then the standing edge-case checklist, but only the ones that are plausible for *this specific problem* - an array problem doesn't need a check for negative tree depth. Then, if time allows, one case shaped differently from anything already tried, to catch a bug the checklist wouldn't.

If you're genuinely out of time, say so rather than silently skipping testing: "I'd want to check the empty-input and duplicate-value cases next, but let me at least trace through the given example first to confirm the core logic." Narrating the gap is itself credit-worthy, even when the clock doesn't allow closing it.

This discipline is the natural close of the narration loop from `thinking-out-loud`: approach, complexity, code, then a visible test pass - skipping the last step leaves the loop half-finished. It also connects to `handling-being-stuck`: a dry run that surfaces a bug you can't immediately explain is itself a form of getting stuck, and the same instinct - narrating what you've found rather than going quiet - applies there too.

The edge cases worth testing are often the same ones worth asking about up front in `clarifying-questions` - empty input, duplicates, negative values. If you asked about them at the start, testing them at the end is just closing the loop you opened.
